content: Healthy eating patterns established during childhood and adolescence are essential for promoting optimal health, growth, and intellectual development in young individuals. These patterns help prevent immediate health issues such as iron deficiency anemia, obesity, eating disorders, and dental caries. Furthermore, they may reduce the risk of long-term health problems, including coronary heart disease, cancer, and stroke. School health programs play a critical role in equipping children and adolescents with the skills, social support, and environmental reinforcement necessary to adopt and maintain healthy eating behaviors throughout their lives. These programs can also help students achieve their full educational potential and maintain good health. This report outlines strategies that are most effective in promoting healthy eating among school-aged youth. It provides comprehensive nutrition education guidelines tailored for school health programs. These guidelines are based on a thorough review of research, theoretical frameworks, and current practices. They were developed collaboratively by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and experts from universities, national organizations, federal agencies, and voluntary groups. School-based programs are uniquely positioned to promote lifelong healthy eating habits. Dietary factors significantly contribute to the burden of preventable illnesses and premature deaths in the United States. National health promotion and disease prevention objectives emphasize the importance of providing nutrition education from preschool through 12th grade. The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) has also advocated for integrating nutrition education into all child nutrition programs and schools. Dietary habits influence both learning potential and overall health. The first national education goal highlights the importance of ensuring children receive the nutrition and healthcare needed to arrive at school with healthy minds and bodies. The recommendations in this report aim to assist school personnel and policymakers at various levels in meeting national health objectives and education goals by implementing effective school-based nutrition education policies and programs. These recommendations are also valuable for students, parents, and professionals in local and state health departments, community-based health and nutrition programs, pediatric clinics, and training institutions for teachers and public health professionals. They complement existing CDC guidelines for school health programs addressing issues such as AIDS prevention, tobacco use prevention, and physical activity promotion. Nutrition education encompasses a wide range of activities designed to encourage healthy eating behaviors. While the guidelines focus primarily on classroom instruction, they are relevant to all components of a comprehensive school health program, including health education, a healthy school environment, health services, counseling, psychological and social services, integrated school-community efforts, physical education, nutrition services, and health promotion for school staff. Although school food service programs play a vital role in providing nutritious meals, this report does not include specific recommendations for food purchasing and preparation. Detailed information on these topics is available in other publications. Additionally, the guidelines do not address the unique nutrition education and counseling needs of pregnant adolescents or young individuals with special needs. The guidelines are grounded in a synthesis of research, theory, and current practices. They align with the principles of national health education standards, opportunity-to-learn standards for health education, and the positions of leading child nutrition organizations. The development process involved expert consultations, reviews of published research, and consideration of national policy recommendations. School-based nutrition education can significantly improve dietary practices that influence the health, growth, and intellectual development of young individuals. Poor eating patterns can lead to immediate health issues such as undernutrition, iron deficiency anemia, and obesity. For example, even moderate undernutrition can have lasting effects on cognitive development and school performance. Chronically undernourished children often score lower on standardized tests, are more susceptible to infections, and experience difficulties in learning and physical activity. Skipping breakfast negatively impacts problem-solving abilities and academic performance. Participation in programs like the School Breakfast Program has been associated with improved test scores and reduced absenteeism. However, many children and adolescents still skip breakfast, highlighting the need for education on its importance. Iron deficiency anemia, the most common cause of anemia in the U.S., impairs the body's ability to produce hemoglobin, leading to fatigue, reduced attention span, and impaired intellectual performance. Female adolescents are particularly at risk. Consuming iron-rich foods and vitamin C can help prevent this condition. The prevalence of overweight and obesity among children and adolescents has more than doubled in recent decades. These conditions are associated with increased risks of chronic diseases, psychological stress, and social exclusion. Promoting physical activity and appropriate caloric intake is essential for prevention and management. Unsafe weight-loss methods, such as meal skipping, fasting, and the use of diet pills, are common among young individuals and can lead to poor growth and delayed development. Education on the dangers of these practices and the importance of healthy weight management is crucial. Dental caries, the most prevalent disease among youth, can result in pain, infections, and tooth loss if untreated. Preventive measures include consuming fluoridated water, using fluoride toothpaste, regular brushing and flossing, and moderating sugar intake. Unhealthy eating patterns established during childhood can increase the risk of chronic diseases in adulthood. Early indicators of conditions like atherosclerosis begin in youth and are influenced by dietary habits. Teaching healthy eating behaviors early in life is critical, as these habits are difficult to change later. Dietary factors contribute to the leading causes of death in the U.S., including coronary heart disease, cancer, and stroke. Interventions promoting healthy eating and physical activity during childhood can prevent these diseases, reduce healthcare costs, and improve quality of life. The Dietary Guidelines for Americans, developed by the USDA and the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, provide evidence-based recommendations for healthy eating. Schools can use these guidelines to educate students and help the nation achieve its health objectives. The Food Guide Pyramid serves as a visual tool to illustrate concepts of variety, moderation, and proportionality in food choices. Despite these efforts, many children and adolescents do not meet dietary recommendations. They consume excessive amounts of fat, saturated fat, and sodium while lacking sufficient fruits, vegetables, and calcium. Education programs must address these gaps and empower young individuals to make informed food choices. Schools are ideal settings for nutrition education, as they reach nearly all children and provide opportunities to practice healthy eating. Teachers and food service personnel can play a vital role in delivering effective programs. By addressing social pressures and promoting positive peer influences, schools can reinforce healthy eating habits and help students develop lifelong patterns consistent with national dietary guidelines.
